Dalton's postulates state that (i) matter consists of INDIVISIBLE atoms and (ii) all atoms of a given element are IDENTICAL in mass and in all other properties.

Hence (B) "matter consists of divisible atoms" and (D) "all atoms of a given element have different properties including mass" are the incorrect postulates.

(A) atoms of different elements differ in mass, (C) compounds are formed when atoms of different elements combine in a fixed ratio, and (E) chemical reactions involve only reorganisation of atoms are all genuine Dalton postulates.

So the incorrect ones are (B) and (D) only.

For \(Fe_{2}O_{3}(s) + 3CO(g) \rightleftharpoons 2Fe(l) + 3CO_{2}(g)\), only the gaseous species appear in the equilibrium expression:
\(K_{p} = \dfrac{p_{CO_{2}}^{3}}{p_{CO}^{3}}\)

A pure solid (or pure liquid) has unit activity, so its amount does not enter \(K\). Adding more \(Fe_{2}O_{3}(s)\) therefore leaves \(Q = K\) unchanged and does NOT disturb the equilibrium.

Adding \(CO_{2}\) raises \(Q\) (shift backward), removing \(CO\) raises \(Q\) (shift backward), and removing \(CO_{2}\) lowers \(Q\) (shift forward) — all three disturb the equilibrium.

Chlorobenzene with NaOH at 623 K / 300 atm (Dow process) gives sodium phenoxide, \(X = C_{6}H_{5}O^{-}Na^{+}\).

Acidification with HCl liberates phenol, \(Y = C_{6}H_{5}OH\).

Phenol is strongly activated towards electrophilic substitution, so with concentrated \(HNO_{3}\) it is nitrated exhaustively at the two ortho and the para positions to give 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid).

Hence \(Z\) = picric acid, which is option (C).

A strong monobasic acid and a strong monoacidic base are both completely ionised in water, so the only net chemical change on mixing is
\(H^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)\), \(\Delta H = -57\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)

Because this single reaction is common to every strong acid + strong base pair, the enthalpy of neutralisation is always \(-57\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\). Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R) is the correct definition of enthalpy of neutralisation, and it is precisely why the value is constant — so (R) is true and is the correct explanation of (A).

Electron counts: \(O^{2-}\) = 8+2 = 10, \(F^{-}\) = 9+1 = 10, \(Na^{+}\) = 11-1 = 10, \(Mg^{2+}\) = 12-2 = 10. All four are isoelectronic, so (A) is correct.

Their nuclear charges are 8, 9, 11 and 12 respectively — not the same — so (B) is incorrect.

For an isoelectronic series the ionic radius falls as the nuclear charge rises (higher \(Z_{eff}\) pulls the same 10 electrons in tighter). Hence
\(O^{2-} > F^{-} > Na^{+} > Mg^{2+}\)
so \(O^{2-}\) is largest (C correct) and \(Mg^{2+}\) is smallest (D correct).

Correct statements: (A), (C) and (D) only.

The four compounds are (A) ethyl propyl ether \(C_{2}H_{5}-O-C_{3}H_{7}\), (B) pentane, (C) pentan-3-one and (D) pentan-2-ol — all \(C_{5}\) skeletons, so boiling point is decided by intermolecular forces.

Pentane: only London dispersion forces — lowest bp (~36 \(^{\circ}C\)).
Ether: weak dipole-dipole in addition to dispersion, no H-bonding (~64 \(^{\circ}C\)).
Ketone: strong dipole-dipole from the polar \(C=O\) (~102 \(^{\circ}C\)).
Alcohol: intermolecular hydrogen bonding — highest (~119 \(^{\circ}C\)).

Increasing order: (B) < (A) < (C) < (D).

Statement I: down group 13 the inert pair effect grows — the \(ns^{2}\) pair becomes progressively reluctant to take part in bonding — so the stability of the +1 state increases \(B < Al < Ga < In < Tl\). For Tl the +1 state is more stable than +3. Statement I is CORRECT.

Ethylene, \(H_{2}C=CH_{2}\), has each carbon \(sp^{2}\) hybridised.

Four \(C-H\) bonds are \(\sigma\) bonds, and the carbon-carbon double bond consists of one \(\sigma\) (\(sp^{2}-sp^{2}\) head-on) plus one \(\pi\) (side-on overlap of the unhybridised 2p orbitals).

Total: \(\sigma = 4 + 1 = 5\), \(\pi = 1\).

The substrate is butan-2-one, \(CH_{3}COCH_{2}CH_{3}\). Treatment with \(N_{2}H_{4}\) gives the hydrazone, and heating that hydrazone with a strong base (KOH) in a high-boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol is the Wolff-Kishner reduction.

Wolff-Kishner converts \(>C=O\) all the way to \(>CH_{2}\):
\(CH_{3}COCH_{2}CH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{3} + N_{2}\)

So \(A\) is n-butane — option (B). The hydrazone options are only the intermediate, and the alcohol option would require a hydride reduction, not this reagent pair.

\(Cr^{2+}\): \(d^{4}\) \(\rightarrow\) 4 unpaired, \(\mu = 4.90\ BM\)
\(Mn^{2+}\): \(d^{5}\) \(\rightarrow\) 5 unpaired, \(\mu = 5.92\ BM\)
\(Fe^{2+}\): \(d^{6}\) \(\rightarrow\) 4 unpaired, \(\mu = 4.90\ BM\)

In a cis alkene the two bond dipoles of the substituents point to the same side of the double bond, so their vector sum is non-zero. In the trans isomer the two identical bond dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel. Hence cis is the more polar isomer — Assertion (A) is true.

For trans-2-butene the two \(CH_{3}\) groups sit on opposite ends of the \(C=C\) axis, the two \(C-CH_{3}\) dipoles cancel exactly and \(\mu = 0\), whereas cis-2-butene has \(\mu \approx 0.33\ D\). Reason (R) is true, and this cancellation is exactly WHY trans is less polar — so (R) correctly explains (A).

In the Bohr model the total energy of the electron in the n-th orbit of hydrogen is \(E_{n} = -R_{H}/n^{2}\), and by the virial theorem the kinetic energy is \(KE = -E_{n} = R_{H}/n^{2}\).

For \(n = 1\): \(KE = R_{H} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ J\).

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\)

\(v^{2} = \dfrac{2(2.18 \times 10^{-18})}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = \dfrac{4.36 \times 10^{-18}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = 4.79 \times 10^{12}\)

\(v = 2.19 \times 10^{6}\ m\ s^{-1} = 21.9 \times 10^{5}\ m\ s^{-1}\)

Mohr's salt is the double salt \(FeSO_{4}\cdot(NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}\cdot 6H_{2}O\).

\(Fe^{2+}\) is a small, doubly charged cation and its aqua ion is appreciably acidic, so in plain water ferrous sulphate hydrolyses:
\(\left[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}\right]^{2+} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons \left[Fe(H_{2}O)_{5}(OH)\right]^{+} + H_{3}O^{+}\)
giving a turbid basic-salt/hydroxide precipitate that spoils the crystals.

Adding dilute \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) supplies \(H_{3}O^{+}\), which by Le Chatelier's principle pushes this hydrolysis equilibrium back to the left, so the solution stays clear and pure crystals separate.

The purpose is therefore to prevent hydrolysis of ferrous sulphate — not to make the medium strongly acidic (only a little acid is used), and \((NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}\) is not the species at risk.

A molecule has zero net dipole moment when its individual bond dipoles cancel by symmetry (or when there are no polar bonds at all).

ZERO dipole moment:
\(H_{2}\) — homonuclear, no bond dipole.
\(CO_{2}\) — linear \(O=C=O\), the two equal dipoles are antiparallel.
\(BF_{3}\) — trigonal planar, three dipoles at \(120^{\circ}\) sum to zero.
\(CH_{4}\) — regular tetrahedral, four identical dipoles cancel.
\(SiF_{4}\) — regular tetrahedral, same argument.
\(BeF_{2}\) — linear \(F-Be-F\), dipoles cancel.

NON-ZERO dipole moment:
\(HF\) (polar diatomic), \(H_{2}S\) and \(H_{2}O\) (bent, lone pairs on the central atom), \(NH_{3}\) (pyramidal), \(CHCl_{3}\) (tetrahedral but with unlike substituents, so no cancellation).

Count = 6.
